templates.stem: If $X=\{2,-1\}$ and $Y=\{4,0\}$, find $X\times Y$. Tap all the ordered pairs that belong to $X\times Y$.
solution: $X\times Y$ is the set of all ordered pairs whose first projection is from X and whose second projection is from Y.
Pair the first element of X, 2, with each element of Y: (2, 4), (2, 0).
Pair the second element of X, -1, with each element of Y: (-1, 4), (-1, 0).

hints.text: Take each element of X in turn and pair it with every element of Y. Check that no element of X is left with fewer pairs than the size of Y.

templates.stem: If $Y=\{4,0\}$ and $Z=\{4,5,-2\}$, find $Y\times Z$. Tap all the ordered pairs that belong to $Y\times Z$.
solution: $Y\times Z$ has first projections from Y and second projections from Z.
Pair 4 with each element of Z: (4, 4), (4, 5), (4, -2).
Pair 0 with each element of Z: (0, 4), (0, 5), (0, -2).

hints.text: Take each element of the first set in turn and pair it with every element of the second set. Count how many pairs each element should have.

templates.notes: Widget X is the book's Y, widget Y is the book's Z. Matches book answer.

templates.stem: If $X=\{2,-1\}$, find $X^2=X\times X$. Tap all the ordered pairs that belong to $X^2$.
solution: $X^2$ means $X\times X$: both projections come from X.
Pair 2 with each element of X: (2, 2), (2, -1).
Pair -1 with each element of X: (-1, 2), (-1, -1).

hints.text: $X^2$ is X crossed with itself. Take each element of X as the first projection and pair it with every element of X.

templates.notes: Reversed-pairs cannot be told apart here because X×X is symmetric, so only missing-pairs is hinted.

gaps.description: Think and discuss 1: list the ordered pairs of y = 2x − 1 for x = 0, 1, 2, giving {(0, −1), (1, 1), (2, 3)}.
gaps.why: The student must produce a set of three pairs. pair_plotter takes a single point and product_builder builds only cartesian products, so no existing kind fits.

gaps.description: Think and discuss 2: plot the three ordered pairs on the coordinate plane.
gaps.why: pair_plotter accepts one lattice point per question, but this part asks for a set of three points.
Every point has a fractional coordinate. pair_plotter only accepts whole-number lattice points, so the instrument cannot reach them.

gaps.description: Drill 4: show the location of X × X for X = [−2, 3], a square region of the plane.
gaps.why: The answer is a continuous region. No existing kind lets the student shade or mark a region of the plane.

records.notes: I made templates for drill-2 A, B and C. Drill-2 D, E and F ask for counts, drill-1 asks for algebra, and the point-reading items (exercise-1, drill-3, drill-4 membership, think-and-discuss-3, think-1 to 3) ask for readings or discussion. None of these is a construction, so they have no template and no gap.

gaps.need_kind: relation builder (select ordered pairs from X×Y that satisfy a stated rule or statement)
gaps.description: pp3u1-2:think-and-discuss-1 — write the statements (which student read which type of book) as ordered pairs from X to Y.
gaps.why: The answer is a proper subset of X×Y chosen by a rule. product_builder grades only the full product X×Y, so a relation's pairs would be marked as 'missing-pairs'. The stem also depends on earlier statements that are not in the exercise text, and the sets contain letters and words, not numbers.

gaps.need_kind: arrow diagram builder (draw arrows from elements of X to elements of Y)
gaps.description: pp3u1-2:think-and-discuss-2 — represent a set of ordered pairs as an arrow diagram.
gaps.why: The student must draw arrows between two sets. No existing instrument connects elements of two sets. pair_plotter selects one lattice point, so it cannot take a set of pairs or give an arrow diagram.

gaps.need_kind: relation builder with arrow and cartesian diagram output
gaps.description: pp3u1-2:drill-1#First — for X={1,2,3}, Y={12,21,47,52} and 'a is a digit of b', write R and represent it by an arrow diagram and a cartesian diagram.
gaps.why: R is a proper subset of X×Y chosen by a rule, so product_builder (full product only) does not fit. The values 12, 21, 47 and 52 are outside pair_plotter's −5..5 grid, and pair_plotter takes only one point. There is no arrow-diagram instrument. The part also asks for three representations.

gaps.need_kind: cartesian-diagram builder (plot several dots for a relation or function)
gaps.description: pp3u1-3:think-and-discuss-1 asks the student to write each relation and represent it by a cartesian diagram. This means plotting a whole set of ordered pairs.
gaps.why: pair_plotter takes only one lattice point per question. The relations are in the book's figure, which a standalone stem cannot refer to, and the stem gives no pairs to read a spec from. Splitting it into single-point questions would not be the exercise, and guessing the pairs would mean inventing the book's data.

records.notes: No templates. drill-1, drill-2 and think-and-discuss-2 ask the student to read a diagram and decide whether it is a function. That is a reading, not a construction, and no existing kind builds the answer. think-1 is an open explanation prompt. LO 3 has no exercises.

templates.stem: Represent graphically the function $f(x) = x + 2$. Drag the two points so the line is the graph.
solution: Put them in a table: (0, 2), (1, 3), (-1, 1).
Plot these points on the square net.
Draw the straight line through them; it crosses the y-axis at (0, 2), not at the origin.

hints.text: Your line has the right lean but sits at the wrong height. Work out f(0) and see where the graph must meet the y-axis.
Check two more pairs in the table: as x increases, does f(x) go up or down?
Each x has exactly one image f(x), so the graph cannot be a vertical line. Use the table of pairs.
Start by finding f(0), f(1) and f(-1) from the rule, then place the points from your table.

templates.notes: Line through (0,2) and (1,3). Inverted slope equals slope here, so not hinted.

templates.stem: Represent graphically the function $g(x) = 3x$. Drag the two points so the line is the graph.
solution: Find some ordered pairs: $g(0)=0$, $g(1)=3$, $g(-1)=-3$.
Put them in a table: (0, 0), (1, 3), (-1, -3).
Plot these points on the square net.
Draw the straight line through them.

hints.text: Compare how far up the line goes for each step of 1 to the right, using your table.
Check g(1) in your table: is the point above or below the x-axis?
Find g(0) from the rule to see where the line must cross the y-axis.
Each x has exactly one image, so the graph cannot be vertical. Use the table of pairs.
Find g(0), g(1) and g(-1) from the rule, then plot those pairs.

templates.stem: Represent graphically the function $\ell(x) = -2x$. Drag the two points so the line is the graph.
solution: Find some ordered pairs: $\ell(0)=0$, $\ell(1)=-2$, $\ell(-1)=2$.
Put them in a table: (0, 0), (1, -2), (-1, 2).
Plot these points on the square net.
Draw the straight line through them.

hints.text: Find ℓ(1) from the rule and check whether the point lies above or below the x-axis.
Use your table: for each step of 1 to the right, how many units does the line move up or down?
Find ℓ(0) from the rule to see where the line must cross the y-axis.
Each x has exactly one image, so the graph cannot be vertical. Use the table of pairs.
Find ℓ(0), ℓ(1) and ℓ(-1) from the rule, then plot those pairs.

templates.stem: Represent graphically the function $f(x) = 5$. Drag the two points so the line is the graph.
solution: Put them in a table.
Plot these points on the square net.
Draw the straight line through them: a horizontal line.

hints.text: Your line is parallel to the right one but at the wrong height. What is the image of every x?
Every x has the same image, so the points have different x but the same y. Does that give a vertical line?
Compare the images in your table: do they change as x changes?
Find f(-1), f(0), f(1) from the rule and compare them.

templates.stem: Represent graphically the function $f(x) = -4$. Drag the two points so the line is the graph.
solution: Put them in a table.
Plot these points on the square net.
Draw the straight line through them: a horizontal line.

hints.text: Your line is parallel to the right one but at the wrong height. What is the image of every x, and is it positive or negative?
Every x has the same image, so the points have different x but the same y. Does that give a vertical line?
Find f(-1), f(0), f(1) from the rule and compare them.

templates.stem: Represent graphically the function $f(x) = 0$. Drag the two points so the line is the graph.
solution: Put them in a table.
Plot these points on the square net.
Draw the straight line through them: it lies along the x-axis.

hints.text: Your line is parallel to the right one but at the wrong height. What is the image of every x?
Every x has the same image, so the points have different x but the same y. Does that give a vertical line?
Find f(-1), f(0), f(1) from the rule and compare them.

gaps.description: drill-5 part 4: represent graphically f(x) = 2 1/2 (a horizontal line at y = 2.5).
gaps.why: line_drawer's intercept b must be a whole number in −5..5; 2.5 is not reachable and the book's number cannot be changed.

records.notes: Only the drill-4 and drill-5 graphing parts are constructions. Drill-1 and drill-2 (identify or state degree) and drill-3 (evaluate or prove) are readings or calculations, so they need no gap. No diagnostics are mapped: intercept-wrong cannot show that the student forced the line through the origin, because the line may be at any wrong height.
